findings: radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp Sink: only the radix bits [44,48) of the stored hash are replaced, and they are replaced with bits from hash(main group columns). Each key's hash is computed the same way every time, so equal keys still get equal hashes. The salt (bits 48-63) and the slot bits are untouched. Probing, resize, repartition and combine all use the stored hash. Distinct finalize re-hashes into the main hash table, so correctness does not depend on the partition layout. With fewer than 4 radix bits, Shift(r)=48-r selects a subset of the prefix-derived bits, which is still consistent.

Prefix column choice: grouping_set is an ordered std::set. The main group indices (< group_by_size) sort before the distinct child indices (>= group_by_size), so the first grouping_set.size() columns of the distinct group chunk are the main groups. This also holds for GROUPING SETS. Picking the wrong columns would only hurt performance, not correctness.

Gates are general: the aggregate must be grouped, have distinct aggregates, and have estimated output >= 4096. A runtime gate on estimated input × row width must also fit within query_max_memory/16. None of these depend on specific tables, literals or scale factors. Ungrouped DISTINCT is excluded.

aggregate_hashtable.cpp: moving sink_count into the pre-hashed AddChunk overload (and into the compressed path) keeps counts unchanged for existing callers. The only difference is that empty chunks are no longer counted, which is harmless. Without the move, the new Sink path would skip adaptivity.

Minor: the author measured about +7% on a heavily skewed in-memory input (90% of rows in one group). The 8 lower radix bits still come from the full hash, which limits how bad the skew can get. Spilling is protected by the memory gate. Both are acceptable tradeoffs.
No changes to timing, settings defaults, tests or the shell. No dead code or duplicated blocks.
